Facebook-kormányzás? Ironikus, hogy a Fidesz pont akkor vádolja Facebook-kormányzással a Tiszát, amikor éppen hogy a fideszesek aktivitása erősödik a közösségi oldalon, és a tiszásoké csökken. Az persze nagyon látványos, hogy a kormány kommunikációjának mennyire hangsúlyos, szinte kizárólagos csatornája lett a Facebook, alig adnak interjúkat, keveset nyilatkoznak, viszont szinte minden fontos bejelentés Facebook-élőben, posztban, sőt, akár kommentben érkezik tőlük. (Amúgy ezt konkrétan a Fidesz kezdte el a Covid alatt, de ez most mindegy is.) Ez egészen logikus, sőt, szinte az egyetlen választásuk, ha olyan kommunikációs terepet akarnak, amit ők kontrollálnak és nagy az elérése. Közmédia még nincs, fideszes stílusú médiabirodalom nem is lesz, a szabad sajtónál meg mindig ott a veszély, hogy kényelmetlen kérdéseket kapnak, vagy legalábbis nem azt kérdezik meg tőlük, amiről éppen nagyon szeretnének beszélni. Marad a közösségi média, saját csatornákkal. Ami persze összességében nem éppen tökéletes a tájékoztatás szempontjából, de még mindig fényévekre van az „Orbán kinyilatkoztatást tesz a Kossuth rádióban” időkhöz képest. Eközben a Fidesz Bár a toplista azt sugallja, hogy a Fidesz összeszedte magát a KO-vereség után, ha megnézzük a tartalmaikat, azt látjuk, hogy még mindig kármentésben vannak, és csak a saját táboruk felé kommunikálnak, azt próbálják egyben tartani. Lassan négy hónapja mondták azt nekik a magyar választók, hogy kösz, ebből nem kérünk, és ehhez képest még mindig abban vannak, hogy ők mindent jól csináltak, nincs szükség önreflexióra, változásra, sőt, a vereség okait se kell keresni, az egy megmagyarázhatatlan, ezoterikus misztikum volt. Ugyanazok az ellenségképek, ugyanazok a mantrák, ugyanúgy harcolni és ellenállni kell, csak egyre kevésbé látni, hogy pontosan miért és hogyan. Mintha kifogyott volna a Fideszből az ötlet, a mondanivaló, a kreativitás, az üzenet. Mintha kifogyott volna a Fidesz, úgy, ahogy van. https://www.dw.com/en/russia-independent.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PFat Prefer DW on Google Launched in 1993, Novaya Gazeta often took on Russia's criminal and political elites Image: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement The Novaya Gazeta newspaper closed its Moscow office on Monday, saying it was not able to continue reporting amid a campaign of state pressure in Russia . The investigative outlet, co-founded by late USSR chief Mikhail Gorbachev, had long been a thorn in the Kremlin's side. In recent years, it ran into increasing roadblocks amid its critical coverage of the Russian invasion of Ukraine . It was branded a "foreign agent," a Soviet-era term resuscitated by President Vladimir Putin 's administration, with officials ordering it to vacate its Moscow offices. Russian banks were also forbidden from processing donations from readers and supporters. The paper had been heavily dependent on this income stream after moving wholly into online publishing, with the transition taking place shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. Russian authorities introduced new wartime censorship rules in the wake of the full-scale invasion. Founding editor Dmitry Muratov shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize for his work with the paper Image: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Nobel Prize winner Muratov calls for free speech 2021 Nobel Peace Prize -winning founding editor Dmitry Muratov issued an appeal for free speech in wartime Russia as journalists gathered in the Novaya Gazeta offices to witness its closure. "Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today," he said. "We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has ceased to function." Russia's government meanwhile sought to play down the significance of the closure, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying it was part of a "rotational process" in a fiercely competitive media landscape. What is Novaya Gazeta? Novaya Gazeta was a flagship for post-Soviet democratic Russia and the era of "glasnost" or openness, also launched by Mikhail Gorbachev. The reformist Soviet leader used some of the prize fund for his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize as seed money for the publication. The paper has built a reputation for fearless reporting, which has also put it in the crosshairs of Russia's wealthy and powerful. Six of its journalists were murdered since the paper was launched in 1993. They included Anna Politkovskaya , who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by Russia's military during its campaigns in Chechnya. An early critic of Putin, she was found dead in her apartment bloc on the president's birthday in 2006. Images published in Russian media on Monday showed the paper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, taking down photographs of Polikovskaya and other reporters murdered in what's thought to be retribution for their work. The paper moved online soon after Russia's invasion of Ukraine Image: AP Photo/picture alliance Last month, when first announcing that the paper would close, Sokolov said the outlet had "been killed." The paper was shutting down after "the Russian authorities — the Russian special services — have forced the editorial team to end its work," he said. Will closure in Moscow mark a definitive end? Muratov called for a ceasefire in Ukraine and urged foreign observers to remember the strength of dissent that endured in Russia, even if it was being pushed underground by censorship laws and other repression or intimidation. "We canot blame the citizens themselves for this," Muratov said, "especially the wonderful, truly remarkable younger generation." "I urge you to distinguish between the Russian authorities and the Russian people," he added. Muratov also called for the release of around 4,000 people he termed political prisoners in Russia. Novaya Gazeta 's leadership has not made it entirely clear whether its closing down in Moscow marks a definitive end to the outlet's reporting, or whether they might perhaps seek to regroup and begin operating in some form from outisde Russia , as several other publications including DW have been forced to in recent years. One of its journalists, Irina Vorobyova, said that the paper's spirit would survive like a "good virus" and would "continue in everyone that was part of it."
